provisioning:Marché d'Aligre.name: Marché d'Aligre
provisioning:Marché d'Aligre.teaser: Street stalls, a covered hall and a flea market on one square in the 12e, and hardly a tour group in sight
provisioning:Marché d'Aligre.story: Place d'Aligre runs three markets at once. Along the rue d'Aligre, open-air stalls stack leeks, clementines and crates of herbs, and traders call out their prices at the end of the morning. On the square, the brocante spreads old cutlery, postcards and chipped bistro plates over trestles. Behind it stands the covered Marché Beauvau, where the cheese, butcher and fish counters keep shop hours. It is the least touristy market in central Paris, the one where people from the 11e and 12e do their weekly shop with a wheeled trolley.
provisioning:Marché d'Aligre.why: Come mid-morning, buy outside first, then walk into the Beauvau hall for cheese and charcuterie before it shuts for lunch.
facts: Open-air stalls Tue-Fri 7:30-13:30, Sat-Sun 7:30-14:30; Beauvau hall Tue-Fri 8:00-13:00 and 16:00-19:30, Sat 8:00-19:30, Sun 8:00-13:30 (Oct 2026)
Between 9:00 and 11:00, when every stall is up; the street is packed away by early afternoon
Seasonal produce at the end-of-market price, the brocante tables on the square, the cheese and meat counters inside the hall

provisioning:Marché des Enfants Rouges.name: Marché des Enfants Rouges
provisioning:Marché des Enfants Rouges.teaser: Paris's oldest covered market, trading since 1615, burned in the night of 11 to 12 October 2026
provisioning:Marché des Enfants Rouges.story: The market took its name from a vanished orphanage whose children were dressed in red, and it had traded behind the rue de Bretagne since 1615, listed as a historic monument in 1982. By 2026 it was half produce and flowers, half lunch counters where people ate elbow to elbow at shared tables. In the night of 11 to 12 October 2026 a fire swept through about 1,000 square metres and brought down part of the inner metal frame; Sud Radio counted 17 businesses lost. Nobody was seriously hurt. The mayor of Paris Centre, Ariel Weil, has promised it will be rebuilt.
provisioning:Marché des Enfants Rouges.why: Do not plan a lunch here this season; check the Ville de Paris page for news of temporary stalls or a reopening date.
facts: Closed since the fire of 12 October 2026; no reopening date announced (Oct 2026)

provisioning:Marché Raspail.name: Marché Raspail
provisioning:Marché Raspail.teaser: On Sunday the boulevard Raspail turns into Paris's best-known organic market, under the plane trees
provisioning:Marché Raspail.story: The stalls line the central strip of the boulevard Raspail between the rue du Cherche-Midi and the rue de Rennes, in the 6e. On Tuesday and Friday mornings it is an ordinary neighbourhood market. On Sunday it becomes the marché biologique: every trader certified organic, selling muddy potatoes, raw-milk butter cut from the block, sourdough loaves, sprouted seeds and galettes cooked on a griddle at the end of the row. The Left Bank comes in a good coat with a wicker basket, and the queue for the galettes is the longest on the boulevard.
provisioning:Marché Raspail.why: Go on Sunday for the organic market and eat a buckwheat galette from the griddle as you walk the rows.

gastronomy:Poilane.name: Poilâne
gastronomy:Poilane.teaser: A two-kilo round of wood-fired sourdough, scored with a P, from the same rue du Cherche-Midi oven since 1932
gastronomy:Poilane.story: Pierre Poilâne opened his bakery on the rue du Cherche-Midi in 1932, and the shop still bakes the loaf he built it on: the miche, a round of about two kilos made with natural leaven, stone-ground flour and sea salt, baked in a wood-fired oven and marked with a cursive P. There are no baguettes and no commercial yeast. The crust is dark and thick, the crumb grey, a little sour, and it keeps for days. Apollonia Poilâne, the founder's granddaughter, runs the house now. Ask for a quarter or a half if a whole one is too much to carry.
gastronomy:Poilane.why: Buy a bag of punitions, the small butter biscuits, and an apple tartelette to eat on the pavement outside.
facts: 8 rue du Cherche-Midi, 6e; a second bakery at 49 boulevard de Grenelle, 15e
Monday to Saturday from about 7:15 to 20:00; closed Sunday by most listings, though one 2026 listing disagrees, so check (Oct 2026)
The miche whole or by the piece, punitions, apple tartelettes; open tartines on the miche at the Comptoir Poilâne next door

gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.name: Du Pain et des Idées
gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.teaser: A crackling slab of bread called pain des amis, and a pistachio-chocolate spiral that sells out by lunch
gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.story: Christophe Vasseur was named one of the city's top bakers in 2008, and his shop on the rue Yves Toudic, a few minutes from the Canal Saint-Martin, became a pilgrimage for bread people. The loaf is the pain des amis, a slab of slow-fermented dough with a burnt, crackling crust. The pastry people cross the city for is the escargot: a laminated spiral rolled with pistachio paste and dark chocolate chips, flaky at the edge and soft at the core. It shuts at weekends, which surprises everyone once.
gastronomy:Du Pain et des Idees.why: Come on a weekday before 9:00 for the pain des amis; the escargots are often gone by lunchtime.
facts: Monday to Friday, from about 7:00 to 19:30 or 20:00 (listings differ); closed Saturday and Sunday (Oct 2026)
The escargot chocolat-pistache, the pain des amis, a seasonal fruit chausson

gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.name: Mori Yoshida
gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.teaser: A Japanese pâtissier on the avenue de Breteuil who makes the French classics with almost no flourish
gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.story: Morihide Yoshida trained at the Park Hyatt Tokyo and the École Nationale Supérieure de la Pâtisserie before opening his shop near Les Invalides in 2013. In 2018 he won the professionals' edition of M6's Le Meilleur Pâtissier. The counter holds the textbook French cakes, a Saint-Honoré, a Mont-Blanc, a Paris-Brest, each made smaller, cleaner and less sweet than you expect. Gault&Millau singles out the Beige, a chocolate and Earl Grey mousse, and a lemon take on the Paris-Brest. The room is white and calm, and the cakes are lined up like exhibits.
gastronomy:Mori Yoshida.why: Order the Mont-Blanc in autumn and taste how little sugar a chestnut needs.
facts: 65 avenue de Breteuil, 7e (Métro Duroc or Sèvres-Lecourbe)
Roughly 10:00 to 19:15; closed Monday, and some listings also give Tuesday as closed, so check (Oct 2026)
The Mont-Blanc, the Paris-Brest, the Beige, the Saint-Honoré

gastronomy:Pierre Herme.name: Pierre Hermé
gastronomy:Pierre Herme.teaser: The rue Bonaparte shop of the pastry chef Vogue called the Picasso of pastry, and home of the Ispahan
gastronomy:Pierre Herme.story: Pierre Hermé opened his first Paris boutique at 72 rue Bonaparte in 2001, a few steps from Saint-Sulpice. Vogue's food writer Jeffrey Steingarten called him the Picasso of pastry, and the line stuck. His signature is the Ispahan, a pairing of rose, lychee and raspberry that perfumes the whole counter, sold as a pastry and as a macaron. The macaron is his other benchmark: trays of them in colours that change with the seasons, and a long glass counter of gâteaux and the praliné 2000 Feuilles beside them. Expect a queue on a Saturday.
gastronomy:Pierre Herme.why: Buy one Ispahan as a whole pastry, not a macaron, and eat it the same day.
facts: Daily, roughly 10:00 to 19:00 or 20:00; listings disagree on Monday and Sunday times, so check (Oct 2026)
The Ispahan pastry, a box of seasonal macarons, the 2000 Feuilles praliné

gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.name: Cédric Grolet
gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.teaser: A lemon that is not a lemon: you cut through the painted skin into cream, compote and sponge
gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.story: The World's 50 Best named Cédric Grolet the world's best pastry chef in 2018, the year Le Meurice opened his pastry shop on the rue de Castiglione. His fame rests on sculpted fruit: a lemon, a peach, a hazelnut, made so exactly, down to the dimpled skin and the stalk, that it looks picked from a market crate until the knife goes in and shows mousse, confit and biscuit inside. In 2019 he added a bakery on the avenue de l'Opéra for croissants and flans. Queues form before opening, and the fruit sells out.
gastronomy:Cedric Grolet.why: Buy one sculpted fruit, whatever is in season, and cut it open at the table so everyone sees the inside.
facts: Le Meurice pâtisserie, 6 rue de Castiglione, 1er; bakery at 35 avenue de l'Opéra, 2e

provisioning:E. Dehillerin.name: E. Dehillerin
provisioning:E. Dehillerin.teaser: Copper pans hung to the ceiling and creaking wooden floors: the cookware house of 1820
provisioning:E. Dehillerin.story: Dehillerin has sold kitchen equipment since 1820 and has stood at the corner of the rue Coquillière since 1890, when this was the edge of the old Les Halles market and its restaurants bought here. Julia Child shopped here while she learned to cook in Paris. Inside it is narrow and dim, the floors creak, and copper saucepans, carbon-steel knives, tart rings, moulds and whisks fill every shelf and hang from hooks overhead. Nothing is arranged for show: you ask, and staff find the size you need.
provisioning:E. Dehillerin.why: Buy a carbon-steel knife or a tinned copper pan; they last decades and cost less here than in a design shop.
facts: 18-20 rue Coquillière, 1er; the Bourse de Commerce is two minutes' walk (its own card)
Monday 9:00-12:30 and 14:00-18:00, Tuesday to Saturday from 9:00 to about 18:00 (the old guide gave Tue-Fri to 19:00); closed Sunday and holidays (Oct 2026, check)
Copper pans, carbon-steel knives, pastry moulds and rings, whisks, mandolines

provisioning:Fromagerie Barthélémy.name: Fromagerie Barthélémy
provisioning:Fromagerie Barthélémy.teaser: A tiny cheese shop on the rue de Grenelle that ages its own wheels and whips its own Fontainebleau
provisioning:Fromagerie Barthélémy.story: Roland Barthélémy built this narrow shop in the 7e into a reference for raw-milk cheese, aged in its own cellars; his wife Nicole ran it after him, and in 2026 it passed to Claire Griffon, who has said the style will not change. The counter is crowded with wheels and wrapped rounds. Ask for the Fontainebleau, a fresh cheese whipped with cream and sold in muslin, or an Ossau-Iraty offered at two or even three ages. Service is brisk and French; a few words of French and a clear ask go far. They do not vacuum-pack.
provisioning:Fromagerie Barthélémy.why: Buy two ages of the same cheese and taste them side by side; it shows what affinage does.
facts: Tuesday to Saturday, about 8:30-19:15; closed Sunday and Monday (Oct 2026)
Fontainebleau, Ossau-Iraty at several ages, seasonal raw-milk cheeses

provisioning:La Grande Épicerie de Paris.name: La Grande Épicerie de Paris
provisioning:La Grande Épicerie de Paris.teaser: Le Bon Marché's food hall: a bakery, a wine cellar, a traiteur and an entire wall of French pantry goods
provisioning:La Grande Épicerie de Paris.story: Across the rue de Sèvres from the Bon Marché department store, the Grande Épicerie is where a galley can fill a whole order in one visit. One floor holds a bakery, butchers, fishmongers, a traiteur counter of cooked dishes and a cave of French wine. The aisles run through tinned sardines and confit, mustards, salt from Guérande, jams, oils and vinegars, and shelves of jarred stocks and sauces. Prices sit above a neighbourhood shop, but the range is unmatched, and it opens on Sunday, when most of Paris is shut.
provisioning:La Grande Épicerie de Paris.why: Use it for the Sunday restock; for bulk couverture, vanilla and nut pastes, G. Detou (58 rue Tiquetonne, 2e) is the pastry cook's shop.
facts: French pantry goods, wine from the cave, the bakery's bread, traiteur dishes for a picnic

avoid:Champs-Élysées terraces.name: Champs-Élysées terraces
avoid:Champs-Élysées terraces.teaser: On the avenue you pay for the address, not the cooking
avoid:Champs-Élysées terraces.story: The cafés and chain brasseries along the Champs-Élysées charge an address premium for the standard French dishes, and much of what arrives has been built from frozen, reheated components. You can spot it before you sit: a laminated menu in several languages, illustrated with photographs, listing twenty-five dishes or more. No kitchen of that size cooks that many plates fresh. One or two streets away the menu shrinks, the languages drop to one, and the food improves.
avoid:Champs-Élysées terraces.why: A short handwritten card that changes is the surest sign of a kitchen that cooks.
facts: Terraces with long, laminated, multilingual photo menus of 25 or more dishes
Walk one or two side streets off the avenue, or into the residential 8e or 17e, and pick a bistro with a short chalkboard menu

avoid:A table with the Eiffel Tower view.name: A table with the Eiffel Tower view
avoid:A table with the Eiffel Tower view.teaser: Within sight of the tower, the view is on the bill and the cooking is an afterthought
avoid:A table with the Eiffel Tower view.story: Restaurants that sell a view of the Eiffel Tower charge what amounts to a view tax: roughly double the normal price for average food and rushed service, because the next table is always waiting. The tower looks just as good from a bench. Look at it first, then walk into the 7e or 15e, where family-run bistros feed the people who live there, or shop along the rue Cler market street and carry the bag to the lawns.
avoid:A table with the Eiffel Tower view.why: A picnic on the Champ de Mars gives you the same view for free, with better bread.
facts: Terrace menus near the tower at about twice the neighbourhood price
Buy bread, cheese and fruit on the rue Cler and picnic on the Champ de Mars, or eat at a family bistro in the 7e or 15e

avoid:The hawker and the photo menu.name: The hawker and the photo menu
avoid:The hawker and the photo menu.teaser: If someone has to pull you in off the pavement, keep walking
avoid:The hawker and the photo menu.story: A host standing out front to lure passers-by onto the terrace, with a photo menu in his hand, is the most reliable red flag in the city, and it is where most reports of tourists being charged more than locals come from. Every Paris café must post its prices where you can read them before you sit, and the bar counter price, prix comptoir, is lower than the terrace price. A room full of French-speaking regulars has no need of a hawker.
avoid:The hawker and the photo menu.why: Read the posted price list before sitting; it is there by law.
facts: A host on the pavement waving a photo menu at passers-by
Order standing at the counter at the cheaper prix comptoir, or sit inside, and choose the room full of regulars

avoid:Things you never ordered.name: Things you never ordered
avoid:Things you never ordered.teaser: Bottled water, a bread basket, olives: they land on the table, then on the bill
avoid:Things you never ordered.story: In the tourist rooms, things arrive unasked: a bottle of mineral water, a basket of bread, a dish of olives, a digestif after dinner. Each one turns up later as a line on the bill. Visitors may also be handed an English menu carrying higher prices than the French one. Tap water is free in France if you ask for it. In an honest place those small touches are either included or priced on the card.
avoid:Things you never ordered.why: Two phrases fix most of it: une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît, and la carte en français.
facts: Water, bread, olives or a digestif set down without being ordered, and an English menu at higher prices
Ask for une carafe d'eau (free tap water) and la carte en français, send back what you did not order, and read the bill

follow:Le Fooding.name: Le Fooding
follow:Le Fooding.teaser: The French guide and magazine that tracks new Paris openings with a critical, unpaid eye
follow:Le Fooding.story: Le Fooding is an independent French restaurant guide and magazine, and the best single feed for what has just opened in Paris and which older addresses still deserve a table. Its reviews are short, opinionated and written in a knowing, slangy French, with a critical, non-promotional eye. It covers bistros, wine bars, bakeries and cheap counters as seriously as tasting menus. Chefs read it; so do the people booking their tables.
follow:Le Fooding.why: Check it before booking anywhere new; if Le Fooding has not covered a room, ask why.
facts: Independent restaurant guide, website, magazine and Instagram feed (@lefooding)
The Paris new-openings pages and the annual guide

follow:Paris by Mouth.name: Paris by Mouth
follow:Paris by Mouth.teaser: Meg Zimbeck's English-language Paris food site, and the summer list of what stays open in August
follow:Paris by Mouth.story: Meg Zimbeck founded Paris by Mouth in 2010 to tell English speakers where to eat and shop for food in Paris, and it now runs as a website, a newsletter and a programme of food tours. The reviews are blunt and practical: which bakery is worth the metro ride, which bistro has slipped. Each summer it publishes its list of restaurants open in August, when much of Paris closes for holidays, and it keeps a running list of what is open on Sunday. Some of the newsletter sits behind a subscription.
follow:Paris by Mouth.why: Read the open-in-August list before any summer visit; it saves the holiday from closed shutters.
facts: English-language food website, Substack newsletter and food tours (@parisbymouth), founded 2010

follow:David Lebovitz.name: David Lebovitz
follow:David Lebovitz.teaser: An American pastry chef and cookbook author who writes about the markets and bakeries he uses every week
follow:David Lebovitz.story: David Lebovitz is an American pastry chef and cookbook author who has lived in Paris for many years and writes about it from the shopping-bag end: the market stall with the best butter, the bakery worth the detour, the neighbourhood bistro that has not changed. His site and Instagram mix recipes with candid opinions on where to eat and what to skip, and his reports read like advice from a friend who cooks rather than a critic who reviews.
follow:David Lebovitz.why: Use him for bakeries, chocolate and markets; that is where his judgement is sharpest.

follow:Paris je t'aime.name: Paris je t'aime
follow:Paris je t'aime.teaser: The official Paris tourist office site: listings, opening hours and tickets with no commission games
follow:Paris je t'aime.story: Paris je t'aime is the website of the city's official tourism office. It is the quickest place to check the practical side of the larder and the sights: market days and hours, shop listings with addresses and phone numbers, museum and monument tickets. The listings are plain and sometimes lag behind a change of hours, but they come from the office itself, not from an aggregator selling placement. Pages run in French, English, Spanish and other languages.
follow:Paris je t'aime.why: Cross-check any market or shop hours here before you send a crew member across town.

follow:MICHELIN Guide France.name: MICHELIN Guide France
follow:MICHELIN Guide France.teaser: The stars, the Bib Gourmands and the full France selection, online and free
follow:MICHELIN Guide France.story: The red guide's France selection lives free on guide.michelin.com, with every starred table, Bib Gourmand and listed restaurant mapped and filterable. The 2026 stars were unveiled on Monday 16 March 2026 at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco, the first ceremony held in the Principality: one new three-star, Les Morainières in Savoie, seven new two-stars and fifty-four new one-stars. The ceremony moves to a different region each year and usually falls in March; the 2027 date and host had not been announced by mid-October 2026.
